preamble: An Act to consolidate and amend the laws relating to the procedure of the Courts of Civil Judicature.

glossary.Code of Civil Procedure: The 1908 Act consolidating and amending the general procedure followed by civil courts in India.
glossary.tribal areas: The territories included, immediately before 21 January 1972, in the tribal areas of Assam under the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution.
glossary.Official Gazette: The government's official publication used to give legal notice of notifications, rules, and other statutory actions.
glossary.Sixth Schedule: The part of the Constitution providing for administration of tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
glossary.decree: The formal expression of an adjudication that conclusively determines the rights of the parties on any matter in controversy in the suit; may be preliminary, final, or partly both.
glossary.decree-holder: Any person in whose favour a decree has been passed or an order capable of execution has been made.
glossary.district: The local limits of the jurisdiction of a principal civil court of original jurisdiction (a District Court), including a High Court's ordinary original civil jurisdiction.
glossary.foreign Court: A court situated outside India that is not established or continued by the authority of the Central Government.
glossary.foreign judgment: The judgment of a foreign Court.
glossary.judgment: The statement given by a Judge of the grounds of a decree or order.
glossary.legal representative: A person who in law represents the estate of a deceased person, including an intermeddler with the estate and a successor on whom the estate devolves in a representative suit.
glossary.mesne profits: Profits a wrongful possessor of property actually received, or could have received with ordinary diligence, plus interest, excluding profits from the possessor's own improvements.
glossary.order: The formal expression of any decision of a civil court that is not a decree.
glossary.pleader: Any person entitled to appear and plead for another in court, including an advocate, vakil, or attorney of a High Court.
glossary.public officer: A person falling within one of eight defined categories of government, judicial, military, or local-authority service or duty under section 2(17).
glossary.District Court: The principal civil court of original jurisdiction for a district.
glossary.High Court: The highest court of civil (and other) jurisdiction in a State or Union territory, to which District Courts and subordinate courts answer.
glossary.Court of Small Causes: A court of summary civil jurisdiction constituted under the Small Cause Courts Acts to try suits of limited value quickly and cheaply.
glossary.special law: A law applicable to a particular subject matter, as distinguished from the Code's general procedure.
glossary.local law: A law applicable only to a particular part of the territory, as distinguished from a law of general application.
glossary.landlord: A person entitled to receive rent for agricultural or other land from a tenant or occupier.
glossary.agricultural land: Land used for agricultural purposes, relevant to rent-recovery remedies and Revenue Court jurisdiction.
glossary.Revenue Court: A court with jurisdiction under local law over suits/proceedings relating to rent, revenue, or profits of agricultural land, excluding an ordinary civil court exercising civil-nature jurisdiction.
glossary.pecuniary jurisdiction: The monetary ceiling on the value of a suit's subject-matter that a given court is competent to try.
glossary.subject-matter: The property, right, or relief that is the substance of the dispute in a suit.
glossary.Provincial Small Cause Courts Act: The Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1887, constituting Small Cause Courts outside the Presidency towns.
glossary.execution of decrees: The formal process by which a court enforces and gives practical effect to a decree or order.
glossary.Presidency Small Cause Courts: Small Cause Courts established at Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay under the Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882.
glossary.Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882: The Act constituting and governing the Small Cause Courts of the Presidency towns of Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay.
glossary.civil nature: The quality of a suit or right that makes it triable as a civil matter, as opposed to a purely religious, political, or non-justiciable question.
glossary.jurisdiction: The legal authority of a court to hear and decide a particular matter.
glossary.expressly barred: A statutory bar on a court's jurisdiction stated in clear, specific words in a statute.
glossary.impliedly barred: A bar on a court's jurisdiction arising from the scheme and language of a special statute, even without explicit ousting words.
glossary.stay of suit: An order halting the trial of a suit, typically pending the outcome of an earlier suit on the same matter.
glossary.same matter in issue: A fact or question directly and substantially contested and requiring decision in both the earlier and later proceeding.
glossary.previously instituted suit: A suit filed before the suit now under consideration, relevant to the section 10 stay-of-suit bar.
glossary.same title: The same legal basis or capacity under which parties claim, used to determine whether privies are bound alongside the original parties.
glossary.res judicata: The doctrine barring re-litigation of a matter directly and substantially in issue that has already been heard and finally decided between the same parties by a competent court.
glossary.former suit: For res judicata purposes, whichever of two suits was decided first, regardless of the order in which they were filed.
glossary.matter directly and substantially in iss: An issue that is a real and material point of controversy actually requiring decision in the suit, as opposed to a collateral or incidental question.
glossary.constructive res judicata: The rule that a matter which ought to have been raised as a ground of attack or defence in a former suit is deemed to have been in issue, even if never actually pleaded.
glossary.competent Court: A court legally empowered, by jurisdiction over subject-matter, value, and territory, to try and decide the suit or issue in question.
glossary.cause of action: The bundle of essential facts that a plaintiff must prove to be entitled to the relief claimed.
glossary.bar to suit: A rule or provision that prevents a party from instituting or maintaining a particular suit.
glossary.competent jurisdiction: Jurisdiction properly and validly held by a court under applicable law, including private international law standards for foreign courts.
glossary.natural justice: The basic fair-procedure requirements of a proper hearing and an unbiased decision-maker.
glossary.fraud: Deliberate deception used to obtain an unfair or unlawful advantage, including in obtaining a judgment.
glossary.international law: The body of rules governing relations between states and, here, the recognised principles applied to determine jurisdiction and recognition of foreign judgments.
glossary.presumption: A rule by which a court infers a fact to be true unless and until it is disproved by evidence to the contrary.
glossary.certified copy: An official copy of a document, authenticated as a true copy by a competent authority.
glossary.lowest grade: The court of the least seniority or jurisdictional rank that is nonetheless competent to try a given suit.
glossary.immovable property: Land and things permanently attached to land, including benefits arising out of land, but excluding standing timber, growing crops, and grass.
glossary.mortgage: A transfer of an interest in immovable property to secure the repayment of a debt or performance of an obligation.
glossary.foreclosure: A mortgagee's remedy extinguishing the mortgagor's right to redeem the mortgaged property.
glossary.redemption: A mortgagor's right to recover mortgaged property upon repayment of the secured debt.
glossary.distraint: The act of seizing property, often to enforce payment of rent or a debt.
glossary.personal obedience: Relief that can be fully satisfied by compelling a defendant's own personal act, rather than by operating directly on property.
glossary.different Courts: Two or more courts whose separate local jurisdictional limits each cover part of the property or subject-matter in suit.
glossary.cognizable: Capable of being taken up and tried by a court, having regard to its jurisdiction over the value or nature of the claim.
glossary.uncertainty of jurisdiction: A genuine doubt as to which of two or more courts has territorial jurisdiction over particular property.
glossary.recorded statement: A court's formal note, made under section 18, recording its satisfaction that jurisdictional uncertainty exists.
glossary.failure of justice: A real prejudice or injustice actually resulting from an error or irregularity, as opposed to a mere technical defect.
glossary.compensation for wrong: Monetary relief claimed for a civil wrong done to a person or to movable property.
glossary.movable property: Property other than immovable property; under the Code it expressly includes growing crops.
glossary.option of plaintiff: The plaintiff's statutory right to choose between two or more permissible venues for filing a suit.
glossary.corporation: A legal entity such as a company, deemed under section 20 to carry on business at its principal or a relevant subordinate office.
glossary.subordinate office: A branch or secondary office of a corporation, relevant for founding venue where the cause of action arises there.
glossary.leave of the Court: Formal permission granted by the court to take a procedural step, such as suing a non-local defendant jointly with a local one.
glossary.acquiescence: A party's conduct amounting to tacit consent or non-objection to a procedural step, such as the venue chosen for a suit.
glossary.objection to jurisdiction: A challenge to a court's competence to try a suit, based on place of suing, pecuniary limits, or local execution limits.
glossary.place of suing: The territorial venue in which a suit is properly instituted.
glossary.earliest possible opportunity: The first available procedural moment, generally at or before the settlement of issues, at which an objection must be raised to preserve it.
glossary.set aside decree: To annul or nullify a decree, whether by appeal, review, revision, or a separate suit where permitted.
glossary.transfer of suit: The movement of a pending suit from one court to another for trial or disposal.
glossary.notice to parties: Formal intimation given to the parties to a proceeding before an order affecting them, such as a transfer, is made.
glossary.Appellate Court: A court exercising jurisdiction to hear appeals from the decrees or orders of a subordinate court.
glossary.application for transfer: A formal request made to the appropriate court seeking transfer of a suit under sections 22-25.
glossary.transfer: The act of moving a pending suit, appeal, or proceeding from one court to another for trial or disposal.
glossary.withdrawal: The act of a superior court taking a pending suit or proceeding out of a subordinate court, for itself or further transfer.
glossary.suo motu: An action taken by a court on its own initiative, without a party's application.
glossary.proceeding: Under section 24, a term extended to include a proceeding for the execution of a decree or order, in addition to suits and appeals.
glossary.Supreme Court: The apex court of India, here exercising the power under section 25 to transfer suits, appeals, or proceedings between States.
glossary.transfer between States: The Supreme Court's power under section 25 to move litigation from a court in one State to a court in another State.
glossary.motion: A formal application made to a court, here the prescribed mode for a section 25 transfer application.
glossary.affidavit: A written statement of facts sworn to be true, used to support applications and, under section 26(2), to prove plaint facts.
glossary.frivolous application: An application devoid of merit or seriousness, attracting a possible compensatory costs order under section 25(4).
glossary.plaint: The formal written statement of a plaintiff's claim by which a civil suit is instituted.
glossary.institution of suit: The formal commencement of a suit, ordinarily by presentation of a plaint.
glossary.summons: A court process calling upon a defendant or witness to appear before the court.
glossary.duly instituted: A suit that has been properly and validly commenced in accordance with the Code's requirements.
glossary.thirty days: The outer time limit from institution of the suit within which a summons must call for the defendant's appearance under section 27.
glossary.interstate service: Service of a summons routed through a court in another State under section 28.
glossary.translation: A rendering of a document into another language, required under section 28(3) when languages of the summons and record differ.
glossary.record of proceedings: The documented history of steps taken by a court in a matter, returned along with an executed summons under section 28(2).
glossary.foreign summons: A summons or process issued by a non-Code-governed Indian court, a Central-Government-established court abroad, or a notified foreign court under section 29.
glossary.reciprocity: The mutual arrangement by which summonses from certain outside courts are served within Code territory, and vice versa.
glossary.discovery: The pre-trial process by which a party obtains disclosure of facts, documents, or objects relevant to the suit.
glossary.interrogatories: Written questions formally put by one party to another, to be answered under oath, as part of discovery.
glossary.inspection: The examination of documents or objects produced by a party for the purposes of the suit.
glossary.impounding: The court's act of retaining custody of a document produced before it.
glossary.witness summons: A summons issued to compel a person's attendance to give evidence or produce documents or objects.
glossary.warrant of arrest: A judicial order authorising the arrest of a person, here to compel attendance under section 32.
glossary.attachment of property: The seizure of a person's property by court order to compel compliance or to satisfy a decree.
glossary.fine: A monetary penalty imposed by a court, capped at five thousand rupees under section 32(c).
glossary.civil prison: A place of civil (non-criminal) detention used to enforce compliance, such as furnishing security under section 32(d).
glossary.security for appearance: A guarantee, often monetary, required from a person to ensure their future attendance before the court.
glossary.hearing: The stage at which a court considers the evidence and arguments in a case before pronouncing judgment.
glossary.interest: A sum payable on a principal amount for the use of money or as compensation for delayed payment.
glossary.principal sum: The core amount of money adjudged due in a money decree, exclusive of interest.
glossary.commercial transaction: Under section 34, a transaction connected with the industry, trade, or business of the party incurring the liability.
glossary.nationalised bank: A corresponding new bank as defined in the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970.
glossary.pendente lite interest: Interest awarded for the period from the institution of the suit to the date of the decree.
glossary.costs: Expenses of and incidental to litigation, which a court may order one party to pay to another.
glossary.discretion of the Court: The court's power to decide a matter, such as costs, based on the facts and circumstances rather than a fixed rule.
glossary.follow the event: The general costs principle that the unsuccessful party pays the costs of the successful party.
glossary.compensatory costs: Costs awarded under section 35A to compensate a party who successfully objects to a false or vexatious claim or defence.
glossary.vexatious claim: A claim made without genuine merit, known by its proponent to be false, and pursued to harass or burden the other party.
glossary.false defence: A defence raised to the knowledge of the party raising it that it is untrue.
glossary.objector: The party who raises an objection under section 35A to an opponent's false or vexatious claim or defence.
glossary.adjournment costs: Costs ordered under section 35B against a party who defaults on a required step or obtains an adjournment, to reimburse the other side's attendance expenses.
glossary.condition precedent: A requirement that must be satisfied before a party is entitled to take a further step, such as continuing to prosecute a suit or defence.
glossary.delay: Postponement in the progress of a suit, which section 35B specifically targets by shifting the cost of the resulting wasted attendance.
glossary.execution of orders: The rule that orders of a court, not just decrees, may also be enforced through the machinery of execution provided in the Code, so far as the nature of the order permits.
glossary.Court of first instance: The trial court that originally heard and decided the suit, as distinct from any appellate court that later reviewed its decision.
glossary.appellate jurisdiction: The power of a higher court to review and revise the decisions of a subordinate court on appeal.
glossary.jurisdictional transfer: The shifting of a case or proceeding from one court to another that has been vested with the requisite jurisdiction to handle it.
glossary.executing Court: The court that actually carries out (executes) a decree, which may or may not be the same court that originally passed it.
glossary.Court which passed the decree: Includes not only the original trial court but, where that court's jurisdiction has ceased or been transferred, the court which would now have jurisdiction to try the suit afresh.
glossary.transfer of decree: The formal act by which a court that passed a decree sends it to another competent court for execution, typically because the judgment-debtor or their property lies outside the first court's local limits.
glossary.sufficient property: Property of the judgment-debtor within the local limits of the transferring court's jurisdiction that is adequate to satisfy the decree, the absence of which is a ground for transferring the decree elsewhere.
glossary.suo motu transfer: A transfer of a decree for execution that a court initiates on its own motion, without a formal application by the decree-holder.
glossary.interstate transfer of decree: The procedure for sending a decree passed by a court in one State to a court in another State for execution, subject to prescribed conditions and rules.
glossary.prescribed rules: The procedural rules framed under the Code (typically in the First Schedule or by rule-making authority) that govern how a particular step, such as an inter-State transfer, must be carried out.
glossary.certificate of execution: A formal certification sent by the executing court back to the court which passed (or transferred) the decree, stating the manner in which the decree has been executed or the extent to which execution has failed.
glossary.failure of execution: The outcome where a decree, or part of it, remains unsatisfied despite execution proceedings, which must be certified to the court that passed or transferred the decree.
glossary.transferred decree: A decree that has been sent by the court which passed it to another court for the purpose of execution.
glossary.same powers: The principle that a court executing a transferred decree has, in relation to that execution, the same powers as if it had itself passed the decree.
glossary.disobedience: The judgment-debtor's or a third party's refusal or failure to comply with a decree or an order of the court, which may attract coercive consequences such as attachment or detention.
glossary.obstruction: Conduct by the judgment-debtor or another person that hinders or resists the executing court's officers in carrying out execution, punishable in the same manner as disobedience.
glossary.onward transfer: The further sending of an already-transferred decree from the court currently holding it to yet another court for execution.
glossary.non-Code-territory decree: A decree passed by a Civil or Revenue Court in a part of India to which the Code of Civil Procedure does not extend, which nonetheless may be executed under the Code's provisions once transferred.
glossary.extraterritorial execution: The execution of a decree in territory beyond the local limits of the court that originally passed it, achieved through the mechanism of transfer to a court having jurisdiction over that territory.
glossary.Revenue Court decree: A decree or order passed by a Revenue Court, which the Code permits to be executed as if it were a decree of a Civil Court, subject to any special rules governing Revenue Courts.
glossary.notification: An official government notification, published in the Official Gazette, that may extend or apply particular provisions of the Code to a specified territory or class of case.
glossary.reciprocating territory: Any country or territory outside India notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette as a reciprocating territory, whose superior courts' decrees can be executed in India as if passed by an Indian District Court.
glossary.superior Courts: In the context of reciprocating territory, the courts specified in the Central Government's notification as the courts of that territory whose decrees qualify for direct execution in India under Section 44A.
glossary.money decree: A decree for the payment of a sum of money, as distinguished from a decree for other reliefs such as possession or injunction; only money decrees (with certain exclusions) from reciprocating territories are directly executable under Section 44A.
glossary.arbitration award: A decision rendered by an arbitrator or arbitral tribunal; sums payable under an award are excluded from the definition of a Section 44A money decree even if the award has been (or could be) enforced as a decree in the original territory.
glossary.execution outside India: The enforcement of an Indian decree through a court situated outside India, permitted under Section 45 only where the State Government has specifically notified that court for this purpose.
glossary.notified Court: A court formally declared, by Government notification in the Official Gazette, to be one to which a particular statutory provision applies.
glossary.precept: A direction issued by the court which passed a decree to another competent court, instructing it to attach specified property of the judgment-debtor as an urgent, temporary measure pending fuller execution proceedings.
glossary.attachment under precept: The temporary attachment of a judgment-debtor's property carried out by a court acting on a precept, which lapses after two months unless extended or converted into a full transfer-based attachment.
glossary.separate suit bar: The rule under Section 47 that disputes between decree-holder and judgment-debtor about the execution, discharge, or satisfaction of a decree must be resolved by the executing court itself, not through an independent fresh suit.
glossary.representative of a party: A person who stands in the shoes of an original party to the suit for execution purposes, such as a legal heir, assignee, or other successor-in-interest.
glossary.auction-purchaser as party: The legal fiction under Explanation II to Section 47 treating the buyer at a court-ordered execution sale as a party to the original suit, so that possession disputes involving them fall within the executing court's jurisdiction.
glossary.repealed section: A section of an Act that has been formally omitted or withdrawn by a later enactment, and no longer has legal effect, though its number may be retained in the text for continuity.
glossary.limitation for execution: The statutory time-limit within which a decree-holder must apply to execute a decree, currently twelve years from the date the decree becomes enforceable under Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
glossary.transferee of a decree: A person to whom a decree has been assigned or transferred by the original decree-holder, who then becomes entitled to execute it.
glossary.equities against original decree-holder: Fair defences, set-offs, or claims that a judgment-debtor could have raised against the original decree-holder, and which remain available even after the decree is transferred to someone else.
glossary.legal representative liability: The principle that a deceased judgment-debtor's legal representative is liable to satisfy the decree only out of estate property that has come into their hands and has not been duly disposed of, not out of their own personal assets.
glossary.duly disposed of: Estate property that a legal representative has properly and legitimately spent, distributed, or applied (for example toward the deceased's genuine debts), and which is therefore no longer available to satisfy a decree.
glossary.modes of execution: The range of methods by which a court may enforce a decree under Section 51 — delivery of specific property, attachment and sale, arrest and detention, appointment of a receiver, or any other manner suited to the relief granted.
glossary.arrest and detention safeguard: The proviso to Section 51 restricting imprisonment for a money decree to cases where the court, after a show-cause hearing, records written reasons finding bad-faith evasion, proven refusal to pay despite means, or a fiduciary breach.
glossary.fiduciary capacity: A position of trust in which a person is legally bound to account for money or property held on another's behalf, such as a trustee, agent, or guardian.
glossary.show-cause opportunity: The mandatory hearing a judgment-debtor must be given before being committed to prison in execution of a money decree, allowing them to explain why detention should not be ordered.
glossary.decree against legal representative: A decree passed directly against a person in their capacity as the legal representative of a deceased person, ordering payment out of the deceased's estate property.
glossary.failure to account for estate property: A legal representative's inability to satisfy the court that estate property which came into their possession was properly applied, which can expose them to execution as if the decree were personal, up to the unaccounted value.
glossary.ancestral property liability: The extension, via Section 53, of Sections 50 and 52's execution rules to ancestral property in the hands of a son or descendant that is liable under Hindu law for a deceased ancestor's debt.
glossary.pious obligation: The Hindu law doctrine under which a son or descendant may be liable to pay off an ancestor's debts out of ancestral property, on grounds of religious and moral duty, independent of personal liability.
glossary.revenue estate partition: The division of an undivided landed estate that is assessed to Government land revenue, carried out under Section 54 by revenue authorities rather than the civil court itself.
glossary.Collector's role in partition: The statutory function assigned to the Collector (or a gazetted subordinate deputed by the Collector) to execute a civil court's decree for partition or separate possession of a share of a revenue-assessed estate.
glossary.dwelling-house entry safeguards: The set of procedural protections in Section 55 restricting when and how an officer may enter a dwelling-house to arrest a judgment-debtor, including a night-time entry ban and special notice to women observing purdah.
glossary.insolvency discharge route: The option given to a judgment-debtor arrested for a money decree to apply to be declared insolvent, potentially leading to discharge from detention if no bad faith is shown and insolvency law requirements are met.
glossary.security for insolvency application: A guarantee furnished by an arrested judgment-debtor, to the court's satisfaction, that they will apply for insolvency within one month and appear as required, which can secure their release from arrest in the meantime.
glossary.absolute bar on arresting women for mone: The non-obstante rule in Section 56 that flatly forbids a court from ordering the arrest or civil-prison detention of a woman to execute a decree for payment of money.
glossary.subsistence allowance: The monthly maintenance amount, fixed by the State Government on scales that may vary by rank, race, and nationality, payable for the upkeep of a judgment-debtor detained in civil prison.
glossary.maximum detention period: The statutory cap under Section 58 on how long a judgment-debtor may be kept in civil prison for a money decree, tiered according to the size of the decretal amount.
glossary.monetary threshold for detention: The minimum decretal amount below which Section 58(1A) forbids any order of civil-prison detention against a judgment-debtor for a money decree.
glossary.release without discharge of debt: The principle that a judgment-debtor's release from civil prison on expiry of the permitted detention period does not extinguish the underlying debt, though it does bar re-arrest under the same decree.
glossary.release on medical grounds: The set of powers under Section 59 permitting cancellation of an arrest warrant, or release from arrest or civil-prison detention, on account of a judgment-debtor's serious illness or, in the case of already-committed persons, infectious or contagious disease.
glossary.warrant cancellation for illness: The court's power under Section 59(1) to cancel an arrest warrant issued against a judgment-debtor before it is executed, on the ground of the judgment-debtor's serious illness.
glossary.attachable property: The broad category of a judgment-debtor's movable and immovable saleable property, and property over which they hold a beneficial disposing power, that is liable to attachment and sale in execution of a decree under Section 60(1).
glossary.exemption from attachment: The list of specific property categories under the proviso to Section 60(1) — such as basic necessities, tools of trade, certain wages and pensions, and insurance proceeds — that are protected from attachment or sale in execution of a decree.
glossary.attachable salary portion: The fraction of a judgment-debtor's monthly salary that may be attached in execution — generally the first exempt slice plus one-third of the remainder attachable (two-thirds exempt) for ordinary decrees, with a larger attachable share for maintenance decrees.
glossary.waiver of exemption void: The rule under Section 60(1A) that any agreement by which a person purports to give up in advance the benefit of an attachment exemption is legally void and unenforceable.
glossary.future maintenance right: A person's right to receive maintenance payments in the future, which under Section 60(1)(n) cannot be attached or sold in execution of a decree because it has not yet accrued as property.
glossary.agricultural produce exemption order: A general or special order that a State Government may publish in the Official Gazette under Section 61, exempting a specified portion of agricultural produce from attachment so that a farmer judgment-debtor can continue cultivation and support their family until the next harvest.
glossary.seizure of movable property safeguards: The procedural protections under Section 62 governing how and when an officer executing process may enter a dwelling-house to seize movable property, including a night-time entry ban and special protection for women in purdah, mirroring the arrest safeguards in Section 55.
glossary.multiple-attachment priority rule: The rule under Section 63 determining which of several courts that have attached the same property under different decrees gets to receive and realize that property and decide related claims — the highest-grade court, or, if equal in grade, whichever attached first.
glossary.Court of highest grade: Among courts that have attached the same property under different decrees, the court occupying the superior position in the judicial hierarchy, which under Section 63 takes priority in receiving and realizing that property.
glossary.private alienation void: The rule under Section 64 that any private transfer, delivery, or contrary payment concerning attached property made after attachment is void as against claims enforceable under that attachment.
glossary.pre-attachment registered contract excep: The exception under Section 64(2) preserving a private transfer of attached property from being voided, where the transfer was made pursuant to a contract both entered into and registered before the attachment took place.
glossary.retroactive vesting of title: The principle under Section 65 that a purchaser's ownership of immovable property bought at an execution sale is deemed to date back to the time of the sale itself, once the sale becomes absolute, rather than to the later confirmation date.
glossary.sale becoming absolute: The point at which an execution sale of property is confirmed under the applicable procedural rules (typically after the period for filing objections has passed without success), after which the purchaser's title is treated as vesting from the original sale date.
glossary.uncertain land interest sale rules: Special rules a State Government may frame by Gazette notification under Section 67 to govern the sale, in execution of money decrees, of land interests too uncertain or undetermined in value for ordinary sale procedure.
glossary.rateable distribution of assets: The proportionate division, under Section 73, of assets recovered from a judgment-debtor among all decree-holders who had applied for execution of their money decrees against that debtor before the assets were received by the court.
glossary.mortgagee surplus exclusion: The rule under Section 73's proviso (a) that a mortgagee or incumbrancer whose secured property is sold in execution is not entitled to share in any surplus proceeds beyond satisfying their own secured interest.
glossary.incumbrance sale proceeds order: The statutory order of priority under Section 73's proviso (c) for applying proceeds from the sale of immovable property sold to discharge an incumbrance: sale expenses first, then the decree amount, then subsequent incumbrances, and finally rateable distribution among other applicant decree-holders.
glossary.resistance to possession: Obstruction by a judgment-debtor, or someone acting on their behalf, that prevents a decree-holder or execution-sale purchaser from actually obtaining possession of immovable property they are legally entitled to.
glossary.detention for obstruction of possession: The coercive remedy under Section 74 allowing a court to detain a judgment-debtor or other obstructing person in civil prison for up to thirty days where they have, without just cause, resisted a decree-holder or purchaser from obtaining possession of immovable property.
glossary.commission (court): A formal delegation by a court to a court-appointed commissioner to carry out a specified task — such as examining a witness, investigating a site, auditing accounts, or effecting a partition — under Section 75 and Order XXVI.
glossary.local investigation commission: A commission issued under Section 75(b) directing a commissioner to visit and investigate a place or site relevant to the suit, and report findings back to the court.
glossary.ministerial act commission: A commission issued under Section 75(g) delegating a routine, non-adjudicatory administrative task to a court-appointed commissioner.
glossary.inter-State commission: A commission issued under Section 76 by a court in one State to a (non-High Court) court in another State, directing the latter to examine a witness residing within its jurisdiction on the issuing court's behalf.
glossary.commission return: The process by which a court that has executed a commission sends the resulting evidence back to the court that issued it, as required by Section 76(2) unless the issuing order specifies otherwise.
glossary.letter of request: A request issued by a court under Section 77, in lieu of a formal commission, seeking the examination of a witness who resides outside India, typically routed through the foreign jurisdiction's own courts.
glossary.reciprocal commission execution: The obligation under Section 78 for Indian courts to execute and return commissions issued by non-Code-territory Indian courts, Central-Government-established courts outside India, or foreign courts, mirroring the procedure for commissions Indian courts themselves issue.
glossary.Union of India as party: The requirement under Section 79(a) that in any suit by or against the Central Government, the party named in the cause title must be 'the Union of India', not a particular ministry or department.
glossary.State as party: The requirement under Section 79(b) that in any suit by or against a State Government, the party named in the cause title must be 'the State' (the relevant State itself), not a particular department.
glossary.two-month statutory notice: The mandatory two-month advance written notice that Section 80(1) requires before instituting a suit against the Government or a public officer acting in official capacity, giving the authority a chance to consider the claim before litigation.
glossary.urgent relief carve-out: The exception under Section 80(2) permitting a suit for urgent or immediate relief against the Government or a public officer to be instituted with the court's leave, without prior notice, though relief can only be granted after the Government/officer is given a reasonable opportunity to show cause.
glossary.curable notice defect: The saving rule under Section 80(3) that a suit against the Government or a public officer will not be dismissed merely for an error or defect in the statutory notice, provided the plaintiff's identity and the cause of action/relief were substantially and properly conveyed.
glossary.public officer arrest immunity: The protection under Section 81(a) shielding a public officer sued for an official act from arrest or attachment of property during the suit, except as part of executing an eventual decree.
glossary.personal appearance exemption: The court's obligation under Section 81(b) to excuse a public-officer defendant from appearing in person where requiring attendance would harm public service, in a suit concerning an official act.
glossary.three-month execution grace period: The mandatory waiting period under Section 82(2) during which execution cannot be issued on a decree against the Government or a public officer, running three months from the date of the decree.
glossary.decree against Union or State: A decree passed against the Union of India or a State Government (or a public officer sued for an official act), subject to the special three-month execution grace period under Section 82.
glossary.alien friend: A foreign national whose country is not at war with India, who under Section 83 may sue in an Indian court as freely as an Indian citizen.
glossary.alien enemy: A national of a country at war with India who, under Section 83, may sue in an Indian court only if residing in India with the Central Government's permission; an alien enemy residing abroad, or in India without permission, cannot sue at all.
glossary.foreign State suing right: The qualified right of a foreign State to institute a suit in an Indian court under Section 84, limited to suits aimed at enforcing a private right vested in that State's Ruler or an officer acting in a public capacity.
glossary.recognized agent (foreign Ruler): A person appointed by the Central Government under Section 85 to prosecute or defend litigation on behalf of a foreign Ruler, through whom all appearances, acts, and applications under the Code are made on that Ruler's behalf.
glossary.sovereign immunity from suit: The general bar under Section 86(1) against suing a foreign State in an Indian court without the Central Government's written, certified consent, subject to a narrow tenant-suit exception and specified consent conditions.
glossary.diplomatic arrest immunity: The absolute bar under Section 86(5) against arresting a foreign Ruler, Ambassador, Envoy, Commonwealth High Commissioner, or specified staff/retinue member under the Code, regardless of consent.
glossary.tenant-suit exception: The proviso to Section 86(1) permitting a tenant of immovable property to sue a foreign State landlord regarding that tenancy without needing the Central Government's consent.
glossary.consent conditions for suing foreign Sta: The four circumstances under Section 86(2) in which the Central Government may grant consent to sue a foreign State: the State itself sued first, it trades locally, it owns local property connected to the suit, or it has waived the immunity.
glossary.Ruler's suit style: The convention under Section 87 that a foreign Ruler is named as party in litigation by the name of his State, unless the Central Government directs an alternative style, such as suing through a named agent, in its Section 86 consent.
glossary.recognised foreign State: A State outside India that the Central Government has formally recognised as such, which is the sole criterion for a State to qualify as a 'foreign State' under Section 87A for Part IV's purposes.
glossary.judicial notice of recognition: The obligation under Section 87A(2) for every court to accept, without requiring separate proof, whether the Central Government has recognized a particular foreign State or a particular person as its head.
glossary.former Indian State Ruler protection: The extension, under Section 87B, of Section 85's representation-appointment machinery and Section 86(1)/(3)'s consent protections to Rulers of former (princely) Indian States, for suits based on pre-26-January-1950 causes of action, as notified by the Central Government.
glossary.interpleader suit: A suit under Section 88 brought by a neutral stakeholder holding disputed money or property, against two or more rival claimants, seeking a court decision on who is rightfully entitled so the stakeholder can safely deliver it and be indemnified.
glossary.stakeholder with no personal interest: The plaintiff in an interpleader suit, who holds a debt, sum, or property claimed by rival third parties but asserts no interest in it beyond recovering charges or costs.
glossary.ADR reference: The court's referral of a pending suit, under Section 89, to one of four alternative dispute resolution tracks — arbitration, conciliation, judicial settlement/Lok Adalat, or mediation — after formulating possible settlement terms.
glossary.Lok Adalat settlement: Resolution of a dispute referred by a court under Section 89(2)(b) to a Lok Adalat, governed by Section 20(1) of the Legal Services Authority Act, 1987 and the rest of that Act.
glossary.judicial settlement: A Section 89 referral track in which the court sends a dispute to a suitable institution or person, who is then deemed a Lok Adalat and whose proceedings are governed by the Legal Services Authority Act, 1987.
glossary.court-annexed mediation: The Section 89(2)(d) track under which the court itself works to bring about a compromise between the parties through mediation, following prescribed procedure.
glossary.special case procedure: The consent-based procedure under Section 90 and Order XXXVI by which parties who agree in writing on the facts can place a stated case before the court solely to obtain its opinion on the legal question involved.
glossary.public nuisance: A wrongful act or condition that affects, or is likely to affect, the public at large or a section of it, rather than causing special damage to any one individual, and which Section 91 allows the Advocate-General or (with leave) two or more persons to sue over.
glossary.Advocate-General: The principal law officer of a State, who under Sections 91 and 92 may institute suits to remedy public nuisances or breaches of public charitable/religious trusts without needing the Court's leave.
glossary.representative suit: A suit instituted by or on behalf of persons having a common interest in the subject-matter, allowing relief for the benefit of a wider class without every member individually suing.
glossary.public trust: An express or constructive trust created for public purposes of a charitable or religious nature, whose beneficiaries are the public or a section of it rather than named individuals, and which is subject to the special suit procedure under Section 92.
glossary.cy pres doctrine: The equitable principle, codified in Section 92(3), allowing a Court to redirect the property or income of a public charitable or religious trust to a new but kindred purpose when the original purpose has been fulfilled, has failed, or cannot practically be carried out.
glossary.scheme suit: A suit under Section 92 seeking the Court's settlement of a 'scheme' — a detailed set of directions — for the proper administration of a public charitable or religious trust.
glossary.removal of trustee: One of the specific reliefs obtainable in a Section 92 suit, by which the Court removes a trustee found to have breached the trust or become otherwise unfit to continue.
glossary.Collector: The chief revenue officer of a district, who under Section 93 may exercise the Advocate-General's powers under Sections 91 and 92 outside presidency-towns, with the State Government's previous sanction.
glossary.presidency-town: A historical term referring to the original presidency cities (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras) where the Advocate-General's own powers under Sections 91 and 92 operate directly, as distinct from other areas where the Collector may be authorized to exercise those powers.
glossary.supplemental proceedings: The interim and interlocutory measures enabled by Section 94 — arrest before judgment, security for property, temporary injunctions, receivers, and other just-and-convenient orders — aimed at preventing a defendant from defeating the ends of justice before the suit is finally decided.
glossary.arrest before judgment: A supplemental proceeding under Section 94(a) and Order XXXVIII by which a defendant may be arrested and required to furnish security for appearance, to prevent him from evading the Court's process or defeating the decree.
glossary.temporary injunction: An interim order under Section 94(c) and Order XXXIX restraining a party from doing a particular act during the pendency of a suit, to preserve the status quo or prevent irreparable harm before final adjudication.
glossary.receiver: A person appointed by the Court under Section 94(d) and Order XL to take custody, manage, and preserve property that is the subject-matter of a suit, pending the suit's final outcome.
glossary.interlocutory order: Any order made by a Court during the pendency of a suit, before the final decree, to regulate the proceedings or protect the parties' interests in the meantime — the residuary category covered by Section 94(e).
glossary.compensation for insufficient grounds: The remedy under Section 95 allowing a defendant to claim, within the same suit, monetary compensation (up to fifty thousand rupees, capped by the Court's pecuniary jurisdiction) where an arrest, attachment, or injunction was obtained against him on insufficient grounds, or where the plaintiff's suit failed for want of reasonable or probable cause.
glossary.malicious institution of suit: The ground under Section 95(1)(b) for compensation, established where the plaintiff's suit fails and it appears there was no reasonable or probable ground for instituting it in the first place.
glossary.pecuniary jurisdiction cap: The upper limit on the amount a Court can award or adjudicate, determined by the value of the subject-matter it is competent to try; Section 95's proviso caps compensation awards at this limit even though the section's own ceiling is fifty thousand rupees.
glossary.first appeal: An appeal under Section 96 from a decree passed by a court of original (trial) jurisdiction, available as of right (subject to the section's own exceptions) without needing to show a substantial question of law, unlike a second appeal.
glossary.original decree: A decree passed by a Court in the exercise of its original (trial-level) civil jurisdiction, as opposed to an appellate decree passed by a court hearing an appeal.
glossary.ex parte decree: A decree passed against a defendant who failed to appear or contest the suit despite due service of summons; Section 96(2) confirms such a decree remains appealable under Section 96.
glossary.consent decree: A decree passed by a Court recording the terms agreed between the parties themselves, which under Section 96(3) cannot be appealed since a consenting party is not an aggrieved party in the ordinary sense.
glossary.Courts of Small Causes: Courts of limited pecuniary jurisdiction established to try small-value money claims summarily; decrees in suits of this nature, below the prescribed value, are appealable under Section 96(4) only on a question of law.
glossary.preliminary decree: A decree that declares and settles the rights of the parties in a suit (such as shares in a partition or accounts) but leaves further steps to be worked out before the suit can be completely disposed of by a final decree.
glossary.final decree: The decree that completely disposes of a suit by giving full effect to the rights already declared in an earlier preliminary decree — for example, by actually effecting a partition by metes and bounds.
glossary.precluded from disputing correctness: The bar under Section 97 preventing a party who did not appeal a preliminary decree from later challenging its correctness when appealing the subsequent final decree in the same suit.
glossary.Division Bench: A Bench of two (or more) Judges of a High Court hearing a matter together, whose decision-making process where opinions differ is governed by Section 98.
glossary.majority opinion: Under Section 98(1), the view concurred in by more than half of the Judges on a Bench, which governs the decision of the appeal where the Judges are not unanimous.
glossary.reference on point of law: The procedure under the proviso to Section 98(2) by which an evenly-split Bench differing specifically on a point of law may state that point and have it decided by one or more additional Judges of the same Court.
glossary.Letters Patent: The royal charter (or its statutory successor instrument) establishing a chartered High Court and conferring on it its constitution and certain special jurisdictions, including historically the right of an intra-Court appeal from a Single Judge — now curtailed by Section 100A.
glossary.misjoinder: The improper joining of parties or causes of action in a single suit who ought not to have been joined together; under Section 99, this alone is not a ground to reverse an otherwise correct decree unless it affected the merits or jurisdiction.
glossary.non-joinder: The failure to join a party or cause of action that ought to have been included in the suit; under Section 99 this is generally not fatal on appeal unless the omitted party was a 'necessary party', which the proviso excepts from the section's protection.
glossary.curable irregularity: A procedural defect, error, or irregularity in a suit's proceedings that did not affect the merits of the case or the Court's jurisdiction, and which Section 99 therefore treats as insufficient, by itself, to justify reversing or remanding a decree.
glossary.necessary party: A person without whom no effective and complete decree can be passed in a suit; non-joinder of such a party is the one exception the proviso to Section 99 carves out from the general rule protecting decrees from reversal for joinder defects.
glossary.merits of the case: The substantive rights and liabilities actually in dispute between the parties, as opposed to procedural or technical matters — the touchstone Section 99 uses to decide whether a defect is serious enough to justify reversing a decree.
glossary.prejudice test: The standard under Section 99A requiring an appellant challenging a Section 47 execution order on account of a procedural error or irregularity to show that the error actually and prejudicially affected the decision of the case, not merely that some technical defect occurred.
glossary.Section 47 order: An order passed by an executing Court under Section 47 determining questions relating to the execution, discharge, or satisfaction of a decree as between the parties to it; Section 99A restricts appellate interference with such orders to cases of demonstrated prejudice.
glossary.execution order appeal: An appeal against an order passed by the executing Court under Section 47, which Section 99A shields from reversal for harmless procedural defects that did not prejudicially affect the case's outcome.
glossary.second appeal: A further appeal to the High Court under Section 100 from a decree already passed in a first appeal, available only where the High Court is satisfied that the case involves a substantial question of law.
glossary.substantial question of law: A question of law that is of general public importance, or directly and substantially affects the rights of the parties, and is not already conclusively settled by binding precedent; the sole gateway ground for a second appeal under Section 100.
glossary.formulation of question: The mandatory step under Section 100(4) by which the High Court must precisely state the substantial question(s) of law it finds involved in a second appeal, before the appeal proceeds to final hearing confined to that question.
glossary.appellate decree: A decree passed by a Court in the exercise of its appellate jurisdiction — i.e., in deciding a first appeal — as distinguished from an original decree passed by a trial court; it is this kind of decree that a second appeal under Section 100 challenges.
glossary.Letters Patent Appeal: A historical intra-High-Court appeal from a judgment of a Single Judge to a Division Bench of the same High Court, exercised under the Court's Letters Patent; Section 100A now bars any such further appeal from a Single Judge's decision in appeals covered by that section.
glossary.Single Judge decision: A judgment and decree delivered by one Judge of a High Court sitting alone in an appeal from an original or appellate decree or order; Section 100A makes such a decision final within the High Court, subject only to further appeal outside the High Court (e.g., to the Supreme Court) where otherwise available.
glossary.non-obstante clause: A statutory clause beginning 'notwithstanding anything contained in...' that overrides any conflicting provision in other laws or instruments; Section 100A opens with such a clause to override contrary Letters Patent provisions.
glossary.exclusivity of Section 100 grounds: The rule in Section 101 that a substantial question of law under Section 100 is the only permissible ground for a second appeal, foreclosing any attempt to argue a second appeal purely on facts or equitable grounds.
glossary.pecuniary bar to second appeal: The absolute bar under Section 102 preventing any second appeal from a decree in a money-recovery suit where the subject-matter did not exceed twenty-five thousand rupees, regardless of whether a substantial question of law might otherwise exist.
glossary.money suit: A suit instituted for the recovery of a sum of money, as distinguished from suits for other reliefs such as possession, injunction, or declaration; the pecuniary bar under Section 102 applies specifically to this category of suit.
glossary.issue of fact in second appeal: A factual issue that the High Court may itself determine in a second appeal under Section 103, but only where it was left undetermined below or was wrongly decided due to an erroneous view of law, and only if the existing evidence on record is sufficient.
glossary.sufficiency of evidence on record: The threshold condition under Section 103 requiring that the material already on the case record be adequate for the High Court to itself decide a necessary factual issue in second appeal, without the need for a remand for fresh evidence.
glossary.appealable orders: Orders of a Court that are capable of being independently appealed, as opposed to the general rule that only decrees carry a right of appeal; Section 104 provides the closed list of such orders under the Code.
glossary.closed list of appealable orders: The principle that Section 104(1) exhaustively enumerates the specific categories of order from which an appeal lies, so that an order not falling within that list (or made appealable by a specific rule) cannot be separately appealed.
glossary.compensatory costs order: An order under Section 35A awarding costs against a party who raised a false or vexatious claim or defence; such an order is independently appealable under Section 104(1)(ff), though only on the narrow ground stated in the proviso.
glossary.leave refusal: An order refusing permission (leave) to institute a suit under Section 91 (public nuisance) or Section 92 (public charity); Section 104(1)(ffa) makes such a refusal independently appealable.
glossary.second appeal from order barred: The rule in Section 104(2) that no further appeal lies from an order already passed in appeal under Section 104 — the appellate order on such matters is final within this section's scheme.
glossary.non-appealable order: An order made by a Court in the exercise of its original or appellate jurisdiction that does not fall within any category independently made appealable by the Code; under Section 105, its correctness can only be raised as a ground of objection in an appeal from the eventual decree.
glossary.ground of objection in decree appeal: The mechanism under Section 105(1) by which an error, defect, or irregularity in a non-appealable interlocutory order can still be challenged — not by a separate appeal from the order, but as a specific ground raised in the memorandum of appeal against the final decree.
glossary.order of remand: An order by which an appellate court sends a case back to the court below for fresh trial, further findings, or other specified action; where such an order is itself appealable and is not appealed, Section 105(2) bars any later challenge to its correctness.
glossary.forum for appeal from order: The rule in Section 106 identifying which Court hears an appeal from an appealable order — ordinarily the same Court that would hear an appeal from the decree in that suit, unless the order was passed by a subordinate court in its appellate capacity, in which case the appeal goes to the High Court.
glossary.appellate jurisdiction forum: The special routing rule under Section 106 that directs an appeal from an order — where that order was itself made by a court (other than the High Court) exercising appellate jurisdiction — to the High Court rather than to the ordinary decree-appeal forum.
glossary.appellate court powers: The bundle of powers conferred on an appellate court by Section 107 — to finally determine the case, remand it, frame and refer issues, or take additional evidence — exercised subject to the conditions in Order XLI.
glossary.remand: The power of an appellate court under Section 107(1)(b) to send a case back to the trial court for fresh trial, further findings, or other specified proceedings, most often exercised where the trial court failed to decide a material issue or wrongly disposed of the suit on a preliminary point.
glossary.framing and referring issues: The power under Section 107(1)(c) allowing an appellate court to frame issues that were not properly framed by the trial court and to send them down to that court for its findings on those specific issues.
glossary.additional evidence in appeal: Evidence taken by, or at the direction of, an appellate court under Section 107(1)(d), which is admitted only within the specific and limited circumstances set out in Order XLI Rule 27, to prevent parties from supplementing a deficient case at the appeal stage.
glossary.procedural extension to second appeals: The rule in Section 108(a) that the procedure prescribed for appeals from original decrees also governs appeals from appellate decrees (i.e., second appeals), so far as applicable and absent a specifically different procedure.
glossary.appeals from orders procedure: The rule in Section 108(b) applying the original-decree appeal procedure to appeals from orders made under the Code or any special/local law, except where that law provides a different procedure of its own.
glossary.certificate of fitness for Supreme Court: A certificate issued by the High Court under Section 109, confirming that a civil case involves a substantial question of law of general importance which, in the High Court's opinion, needs to be decided by the Supreme Court, thereby entitling the party to appeal as of right rather than by discretionary leave.
glossary.substantial question of law of general i: The specific, elevated threshold required for a Section 109 certificate — beyond an ordinary substantial question of law under Section 100, it must additionally be of general importance transcending the individual case.
glossary.constitutional appeal to Supreme Court: The broader constitutional framework (Articles 132-136 of the Constitution) within which Section 109's certificate mechanism operates, and which also independently supplies the discretionary Special Leave Petition route under Article 136.
glossary.omitted section: A section of the Code that has been formally deleted by a subsequent amending Act, leaving only its number as a placeholder in the Code's numbering scheme, with no continuing legal effect.
glossary.savings clause: A statutory provision, such as Section 112, that expressly preserves specified powers, rules, or categories of proceeding from being affected by the surrounding law — here, preserving the Supreme Court's constitutional powers and its own procedural rules, and excluding criminal, admiralty, and Prize Court matters from the Code's appeal provisions.
glossary.Article 136 special leave: The Supreme Court's discretionary constitutional power under Article 136 to grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, order, or sentence of any court or tribunal in India, expressly preserved from being cut down by anything in the Code under Section 112(1)(a).
glossary.Prize Court exclusion: The exclusion, under Section 112(2), of appeals from orders and decrees of Prize Courts (courts adjudicating the disposal of enemy property captured in war) from the Code's ordinary civil appeal provisions.
glossary.reference to High Court: The procedure under Section 113 by which a subordinate court, while a case is still pending before it, states a case and refers a specific question to the High Court for its opinion, subject to the conditions prescribed in Order XLVI.
glossary.case stated: The formal document in which a subordinate court making a reference under Section 113 sets out the relevant facts, the question involved, and (where the reference is mandatory under the proviso) its own opinion and reasons, for the High Court's consideration.
glossary.mandatory reference on constitutional va: The obligatory reference required by the proviso to Section 113 where a subordinate court itself considers a statute, ordinance, or regulation invalid or inoperative but no High Court or the Supreme Court has yet so declared — the subordinate court must refer the question rather than decide it alone.
glossary.review of judgment: The remedy under Section 114 by which a person aggrieved by a decree or order may apply to the very same Court that passed it, asking that Court to reconsider its own decision on the specific grounds set out in Order XLVII Rule 1.
glossary.same court reconsideration: The distinguishing feature of review under Section 114 — unlike an appeal (heard by a higher court) or a revision (heard by the High Court), a review application is made to, and decided by, the identical Court that passed the original decree or order.
glossary.review application: The formal application by which a party invokes the Court's power under Section 114 and Order XLVII to reconsider its own decree or order, available where an appeal lay but was not filed, where no appeal lies at all, or on a Small Cause Court reference decision.
glossary.revisional jurisdiction: The supervisory power of the High Court under Section 115 to call for and examine the record of a case decided by a subordinate court, confined strictly to correcting jurisdictional errors rather than re-examining the merits.
glossary.jurisdictional error: An error falling within one of the three categories in Section 115(1)(a)-(c) — exercising jurisdiction not vested by law, failing to exercise jurisdiction that is vested, or exercising jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity — as distinct from an ordinary error of fact or law made within jurisdiction, which is not revisable.
glossary.material irregularity: A serious procedural defect in how a subordinate court exercised its jurisdiction (as opposed to a defect in the decision on the merits), which under Section 115(1)(c) can justify the High Court's revisional interference.
glossary.no automatic stay: The rule in Section 115(3) that merely filing a revision petition does not by itself stay the suit or proceeding below — a party must separately and specifically apply for, and obtain, a stay order from the High Court.
glossary.case decided: The phrase construed by the Explanation to Section 115 to include not only final decisions but also any order, including an order deciding an issue, made in the course of a still-pending suit or other proceeding — thereby bringing interlocutory orders within the scope of revisable 'cases'.
glossary.Part IX application: The scope-limiting rule in Section 116 confining Part IX's special provisions (Sections 117-120) to Chartered High Courts and Judicial Commissioners' Courts, rather than to every High Court in India.
glossary.Judicial Commissioner's court: A historical judicial authority, treated as a High Court for certain Code purposes, that formerly exercised civil jurisdiction in some Union territories before their court systems were reorganized.
glossary.applicability of the Code to High Courts: The general rule in Section 117 that the Code applies to High Courts, subject to the special modifications and exceptions carved out for their ordinary original civil jurisdiction elsewhere in Part IX.
glossary.taxation of costs: The formal process by which a Court's officer (the taxing officer) scrutinizes and quantifies the exact amount of costs a successful party is entitled to recover, as distinct from the Court's earlier order that costs be awarded in principle.
glossary.execution before cost ascertainment: The facility under Section 118 allowing a High Court decree to be executed for the substantive relief granted even before the precise quantum of costs has been finally taxed and ascertained.
glossary.right of audience: The entitlement to appear and be heard before a Court as an advocate or authorized representative; Section 119 confines this right in the High Court's original civil jurisdiction to persons legally authorized to practise there.
glossary.authorized legal representative: A person who, under Section 119, is legally entitled to address the High Court in its original civil jurisdiction on behalf of a party — ordinarily an enrolled advocate — as opposed to an unauthorized layperson.
glossary.excluded provisions for High Court origi: The list of Code sections (chiefly those on territorial jurisdiction of subordinate courts) that Section 120 declares inapplicable to a High Court exercising its own ordinary original civil jurisdiction.
glossary.territorial jurisdiction sections exclud: Sections 16 to 20 of the Code, dealing with the territorial jurisdiction of subordinate courts over suits, which Section 120 disapplies to a High Court's original civil jurisdiction since a Chartered High Court's original jurisdiction rests on its own charter/Letters Patent, not these sections.
glossary.First Schedule rules: The body of procedural Rules (organized into Orders I-LI) appended to the Code as its First Schedule, which under Section 121 have the same binding, statutory force as the Sections themselves unless validly altered under the Code's rule-making powers.
glossary.statutory force of rules: The principle under Section 121 that the First Schedule's Orders and Rules are not mere administrative guidance but carry the full force of law, exactly as if enacted in the body of the Code.
glossary.rule-making power of High Courts: The authority conferred by Sections 122 and 129/130 permitting specified High Courts to alter, annul, or add to the Rules in the First Schedule, adapting procedure to local conditions without needing fresh legislation.
glossary.previous publication requirement: The procedural safeguard under Section 122's proviso requiring that a High Court's proposed rule changes be previously published for objections and suggestions before being finally made, ensuring stakeholder input.
glossary.superintendence over subordinate courts: The High Court's supervisory authority over the courts subordinate to it, which underlies and justifies its power under Section 122 to prescribe binding procedural rules for those courts.
glossary.Rule Committee: A committee constituted under Section 123 in certain States, comprising the Chief Justice and other Judges and members, to consider and formulate proposals for amending the First Schedule's Rules before the High Court acts on them.
glossary.rule-making composition: The specific membership structure prescribed by Section 123 for a Rule Committee — Judges of the High Court together with other persons the State Government may nominate or the High Court may co-opt.
glossary.High Court nomination of members: The power, alongside State Government nomination, by which a High Court may itself select certain members to sit on its Rule Committee under Section 123.
glossary.Rule Committee report: The formal report that a Rule Committee constituted under Section 123 must prepare and submit to the High Court under Section 124, setting out its proposals for rule changes, before the High Court exercises its rule-making power.
glossary.mandatory consideration before rule-maki: The requirement under Section 124 that a High Court to which Section 123 applies must consider the Rule Committee's report before making, altering, or annulling any First Schedule rule — a procedural precondition to validity.
glossary.rule-making by other High Courts: The parallel rule-making power conferred by Section 125 on High Courts not covered by Sections 122-124, allowing them too to adapt the First Schedule Rules, subject to any conditions the State Government may impose.
glossary.State Government-determined conditions: Conditions and restrictions that a State Government may impose, under Section 125, on a High Court's exercise of its rule-making power in respect of courts subordinate to it.
glossary.cross-adoption of rules: The facility recognized under Section 125 by which a High Court may adopt, with or without modification, rules already framed by another High Court, rather than drafting entirely fresh rules.
glossary.State Government approval of rules: The requirement under Section 126 that rules made under Sections 122-125 do not take effect until approved by the State Government (or, for matters within its domain, the Central Government), acting as a check on the High Court's delegated rule-making power.
glossary.Central Government approval: The alternative or additional approving authority under Section 126 for rules touching subjects falling within the Central Government's competence, as opposed to purely State subjects approved by the State Government.
glossary.Official Gazette publication: The formal requirement under Section 127 that rules made under the Code be published in the Official Gazette before they can take legal effect, giving the public constructive notice of the change.
glossary.effective date of rules: The point at which validly made and approved procedural rules become legally binding, fixed by Section 127 as the date of their publication in the Official Gazette (or a later date the rule itself specifies).
glossary.scope of rule-making power: The illustrative, non-exhaustive list of procedural subjects set out in Section 128 (such as pleadings, execution, appeals, and costs) on which High Courts may make rules under their Section 122/125 powers, without limiting that power to only these listed matters.
glossary.summary procedure: An abbreviated, expedited mode of trial or disposal — for instance, for suits on negotiable instruments or other liquidated claims — that rules made under Section 128 may prescribe in place of the Code's ordinary, fuller procedure.
glossary.originating summons: A simplified procedure for commencing certain classes of suit (typically involving construction of a will, deed, or other document with no substantial factual dispute) that rules made under Section 128 may provide for, bypassing the need for a full plaint and written statement.
glossary.consolidation of suits: The procedural device, which rules under Section 128 may regulate, by which two or more related suits pending before a Court are combined and tried together to avoid multiplicity and inconsistent findings.
glossary.original side rules: Rules framed by a Chartered High Court under Section 129 to regulate the procedure of its own ordinary original civil jurisdiction (its 'Original Side'), distinct from rules governing the appellate or subordinate courts.
glossary.Letters Patent consistency: The requirement, inherent in Section 129, that a Chartered High Court's original-side rules must not conflict with its own Letters Patent, which is the constitutional source of that original jurisdiction.
glossary.chartered High Court procedure: The distinct procedural regime available to the presidency High Courts (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras) and other Chartered High Courts for their original civil jurisdiction, framed under Section 129 rather than the ordinary Code procedure that governs subordinate courts.
glossary.non-procedural rule-making: The narrower rule-making power under Section 130, available to High Courts other than the Chartered ones, confined to matters other than procedure (e.g., administrative and supervisory matters) in relation to courts subject to their superintendence.
glossary.Article 227 superintendence: The constitutional power of superintendence that a High Court exercises over courts and tribunals within its jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution, which underlies its Section 130 rule-making authority over non-procedural matters.
glossary.presidency town exclusion: The carve-out under Section 130 excluding the presidency-towns (where Chartered High Courts already have original-side rule-making power under Section 129) from the scope of the non-procedural rule-making power given to other High Courts.
glossary.publication of Section 129/130 rules: The requirement under Section 131 that rules made by High Courts under Sections 129 or 130 must similarly be published (generally in the Official Gazette) before taking effect, paralleling the Section 127 requirement for rules made under Sections 122-125.
glossary.force of law upon publication: The principle, common to Sections 127 and 131, that a validly made procedural rule acquires binding legal effect only from the point of its proper publication, not from the date it was merely framed or approved.
glossary.exemption from personal appearance: The protection under Sections 132 and 133 excusing certain categories of persons from having to personally appear in Court, allowing them instead to be represented or examined through alternative means such as commission.
glossary.purdanashin women: Women who, by reason of custom, observe strict seclusion (purdah) from appearing in public before men outside their family; Section 132 exempts such women from compulsory personal appearance in Court.
glossary.exemption from personal appearance for h: The specific protection under Section 133 excusing the President, Vice-President, Speaker, Ministers, Governors, Judges, and certain other high constitutional functionaries from being compelled to personally attend Court, in recognition of their office.
glossary.examination by commission cost: The rule attached to Section 133's exemption that where a protected office-holder is examined via a commission rather than in open Court, the costs of that commission are ordinarily borne as the Court directs, often by the party seeking the examination.
glossary.arrest procedure extension: The rule under Section 134 extending specified procedural safeguards (drawn from Sections 55, 57, and 59) governing arrest in execution of a decree to arrests made under other civil process as well.
glossary.Sections 55/57/59 applicability: The specific cross-reference in Section 134 applying the substantive protections found in Sections 55 (grounds and conditions for arrest and detention), 57 (subsistence allowance), and 59 (release on ground of illness) to arrests made otherwise than strictly in execution of a decree.
glossary.judicial officer arrest immunity: The protection under Section 135 shielding Judges, and certain other judicial and law officers, from arrest under civil process while going to, presiding in, or returning from Court, to preserve the independence and dignity of judicial functions.
glossary.tribunal-attendance arrest exemption: The protection under Section 135 extending to persons required to attend as parties or witnesses before a Court, tribunal, or other legal authority, exempting them from civil arrest while going to, attending, or returning from such proceedings.
glossary.immediate execution exception: The proviso to Section 135 clarifying that its arrest-immunity protection does not prevent execution of a decree or order made against the very person in the specific proceeding they are attending.
glossary.legislator arrest immunity: The protection under Section 135A shielding members of legislative bodies (Parliament and State Legislatures) from arrest and detention under civil process during specified periods connected with sessions and meetings of the body to which they belong.
glossary.forty-day protection window: The specific duration prescribed by Section 135A — forty days before and after a session or meeting of the relevant legislative body, in addition to the session/meeting itself — during which a member is immune from civil arrest and detention.
glossary.re-arrest liability: The rule under Section 135A that a member of a legislative body released from civil arrest or detention because of the protected period remains liable to be re-arrested and detained once that protected period has ended.
glossary.outside-district process: Process (for arrest of a person or attachment of property) that needs to be executed in a district other than the one where the issuing Court is situated, addressed by Section 136's alternative routing to the Court where the person/property currently is.
glossary.arrest or attachment process: Court process directing the arrest of a person or the attachment of property, which under Section 136 may be sent directly to the Court within whose local limits the person or property is currently found, rather than to the Court of ordinary residence/situs.
